meta.title: Sleep History Logic Map
meta.subtitle: Does sleep keep an internal history, and how does it cope with disturbance?
meta.scope: 6 implanted rats (SF07–SF12) in an outdoor paddock, 2026-08-30 → 09-11 19:40 (the five females after that are excluded); 169 sessions → 129 records, 1227 h. Automatic 1-s scores (FINAL); no manual epoch scoring (κ).
meta.focus_note: Link being built: an individual's own sleep history ↔ who keeps sleeping and who wakes in the same group event

nodes.title: Does sleep keep an internal history, and does it reorganise NREM/REM to cope with disturbance?
nodes.text: Core question (the user, 2026-10-08). The direction to connect: an individual's own sleep history, and why in the same group event some animals keep sleeping while others wake. Framing agreed 2026-10-07: an internal rule that organises sleep states, carries history and is updated during wakes; not a fixed timetable; it has to survive interruptions.

nodes.title: Sleep is interrupted all the time, yet daily amounts are regular
nodes.text: Over 08-31 → 09-06 (all 6 rats): NREM 9.7 ± 0.2 h and REM 1.8 ± 0.1 h per 24 h; REM 15.9 % of sleep. 82 % of REM-to-REM intervals contain some wake; the median wake bout lasts 23 s.

nodes.title: Internal regulation that carries history
nodes.text: Sleep follows rules that carry a short summary of recent sleep (the PI's scheduling hypothesis as reframed with the user, 2026-10-07). Pattern level: says nothing about the neural implementation. How wakes update the summary is a separate, candidate question (Q4).

sources.anchor: internal rule that organises sleep states

nodes.title: No carried history: clock, conditions and the current state are enough
nodes.text: Transitions follow the circadian clock, the conditions and the current state only (a fixed timetable or memoryless switching). The null against every history claim.

changes.what: Source re-cited after the audit's #21 wording fix (commit a3ca36e).

nodes.title: Stage trade-off (the PI's first formulation): one stage longer → the other shorter
nodes.text: Within a sleep cycle, stages are allocated against each other like jobs on a processor: a longer REM shortens the following NREM, or a longer NREM shortens the next REM.

nodes.title: Sleep budget: deviations are made up later (hours to a day)
nodes.text: A shortfall of REM or NREM is followed by a surplus, so amounts are balanced over hours or over the 24 h (homeostatic payback). Shown in the literature only after deprivation, never in undisturbed data.

sources.anchor: A budget has been shown only after deprivation

nodes.title: A neural scheduler allocates NREM and REM time
nodes.text: The mechanistic reading: a brain circuit schedules sleep states like a job scheduler. Needs an intervention and neural content; natural data can only test predictive dependence on history.

nodes.title: #21 The brain schedules sleep — unresolved by design
nodes.text: Natural data with no intervention beyond the battery rounds cannot show a scheduling mechanism. Allowed (corrected 2026-10-09): history-dependent, interruption-sensitive rules that reproduce the daily totals without a daily budget, consistent with an internal regulation of REM entry rather than a fixed timetable; a REM repayment only after handled interruptions (candidate); no day-to-day balance shown.
nodes.allowed: The data show history-dependent, interruption-sensitive rules — and daily REM and NREM totals that those rules reproduce without a daily budget — consistent with an internal regulation of REM entry rather than a fixed timetable. A repayment of REM has been seen only after handled interruptions (candidate); no day-to-day balance was shown.
nodes.forbidden: Mechanistic 'scheduler' wording. 'Balancing / balanced over the day' (#13 withdrawn).

nodes.title: Rules that carry history: yes. A fixed timetable: no. A scheduler mechanism: not testable here.
nodes.text: Established: sleep follows rules that carry history. REM becomes more likely the more NREM has built up since the last REM; brief awakenings do not erase that build-up; the night limits how often REM starts, not how long it lasts. Candidate: a long wake pushes the next REM back without resuming the earlier progress; sleep is balanced between night and day. Not shown: a fixed timetable, minute-for-minute compensation, outside causes of awakenings, a mechanism.

nodes.title: Organising idea: only REM entry is regulated — by the count since the last REM and a smooth daily curve
nodes.text: Proposed by the logic audit (Fable, 2026-10-08) and kept in the claim audit's synthesis as an interpretation: REM entry is the regulated knob (#14: the night limits entry, not duration), REM duration and REM exits follow no history, and daily totals are regular because the inputs are regular, not because a budget is enforced. #40 is consistent with it (the generative model has history on REM entry only), but REM-bout duration and REM exits were never tested for regulation (step F H7, H8): stayed proposed until r8. Step F1 (r8): the same count predicts the next REM bout's duration (#48, established association) and night REM bouts end in waking more often at matched length (#49, candidate, FINAL strong) — the 'REM duration and exits follow no history' half does not hold as stated; the REM-entry half stands (h.model.count). The 'regular inputs, no budget' half is now h.core.regular_inputs. The claim audit's synthesis was rewritten on 2026-10-10 by its owner (c.entry_only_wording resolved): 'only REM entry is regulated' is marked superseded by #48 / #49, as the plan anticipated; the organising idea now reads that the count sets REM entry and also predicts the next REM bout's length, read through a smooth daily curve, with night REM ending in waking more often (#49, Candidate). This node keeps the original idea and its history: weakened for the REM-maintenance half.

nodes.title: Rules that carry history: yes. No day-to-day balance (a drift). Organising idea under test: only REM entry is regulated.
nodes.text: Established: REM entry tracks the NREM accumulated since the last REM; brief awakenings do not erase that history; the night limits how often REM starts, not how long it lasts; over the 12 days all rats moved sleep from night into day (#30, a drift, not a balance). Candidate: a wake ≥ 7 min is not resumed; at night longer wakes delay REM further; the night lowers REM entry even after equally short wakes; REM missed before a morning round is repaid, specifically REM. Interpretation to test (the plan's scheduler model): only REM entry is regulated, by a count, a day/night gain and perhaps a slow REM deficit. Not shown: a day-to-day 24-h balance, a fixed timetable, an NREM rebound proportional to wake length, outside causes of awakenings, a mechanism.

nodes.title: Rules that carry history generate the daily sleep without a budget; a REM repayment appears only after handling
nodes.text: Established: REM entry is set by one count of NREM since the last REM (emptied by REM, fading over a wake), read through a daily curve (smooth, with no light switch: candidate, #35) that lowers entry about three-fold at night at the same count and prior wake; brief wakes keep the history, wakes ≥ 7 min are not resumed; simulated from these rules, conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps, the model reproduces daily REM and NREM and their day-to-day variation without any budget (#40), and beats a momentum model (#41); an NREM homeostat adds nothing to NREM endings (#42). Candidate: REM missed before a morning round is repaid by a process the rules do not contain, seen only after handled interruptions (#43); handling, dawn timing and the round's sleep loss are not separated, and a general slow REM deficit is neither shown nor excluded (low power). The budget is not needed for the daily totals but was never fitted ('there is no REM budget' is forbidden). Interpretation still to test: only REM entry is regulated. Not testable here: a neural scheduler.

nodes.title: Rules that carry history generate the daily sleep without a budget; the same count also predicts REM duration; the rules miss the acute response to a handled round
nodes.text: Established: REM entry is set by one count of NREM since the last REM (emptied by REM, fading over a wake), read through a daily curve (smooth, with no light switch: candidate, #35) that lowers entry about three-fold at night at the same count and prior wake; brief wakes keep the history, wakes ≥ 7 min are not resumed; simulated from these rules, conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps, the model reproduces daily REM and NREM and their day-to-day variation without any budget (#40) and beats a momentum model (#41); an NREM homeostat adds nothing to NREM endings (#42); REM already taken that day adds nothing to REM entry (#52, no quota in the transitions). The same count also predicts how long the next REM lasts (#48, association), and brief awakenings are most frequent right after a REM (#51): 'only REM entry is regulated' does not hold as stated (REM duration follows the count; night REM exits differ, #49 candidate) — the audit's organising idea, rewritten by its owner on 2026-10-10, now reads that the count sets REM entry and also predicts the next REM's length, read through a smooth daily curve (an interpretation). After a handled battery round, rules that never saw one predict the amounts of REM and NREM over 3–6 h (#47) but not the acute response: for about an hour NREM ends in waking ~1.3–1.4× as often as predicted (#44) and the first REM comes later in wall time (#47; its origin is the q.perturbation branch). Candidate: REM missed before a morning round is repaid by a process the rules do not contain, seen only after handled interruptions and only on fixed thresholds (#43; part G: handling, dawn timing and the round's sleep loss still not separated, power). The budget is not needed for the daily totals but was never fitted ('there is no REM budget' is forbidden); that the totals are regular because the inputs are regular is shown only conditional on the observed long wakes (#40) — the unconditional test is the long-wake generative model (h.core.regular_inputs). Not testable here: a neural scheduler.

nodes.text: H7: ln REM-bout duration on the count at onset, dark, ln prior wake, temperature and group size (the planned C3 that was never run). H10: are sequential cycles rarer at night through the gain or through interruptions (second REM within 135 s vs MA count). Sequence-only; pass rules as in the plan; pass2med for night vs day.

nodes.text: Recent sleep history improves held-out prediction of how NREM ends in every fold and every rat, with a large effect at the bout scale (4 % vs 67 % REM endings). The no-history null is weakened. This is predictive dependence on history, not a mechanism.

nodes.text: The current state and the quantities accumulated since the last REM capture the predictive gain; distant windows add nothing within records. Fragmentation is borderline. nodes.title: One running count since the last REM, with the current state, carries the history; fragmentation adds nothing beyond it

nodes.title: REM propensity builds with NREM accumulated since the last REM (refractory build-up)
nodes.text: Mice and humans: a refractory period after REM, then rising REM propensity (Park 2021, Bassi 2009, Ginsberg 2024).

nodes.title: Deeper recent NREM favours REM; shallow NREM favours waking
Wake accumulated since the last REM lowers the REM drive (REM pressure dissipates in wake)
nodes.text: The predictive fact (v2 #2, candidate): the more wake since the last REM, the less likely an NREM bout ends in REM. This hypothesis reads it as a lower REM drive.

nodes.title: A longer REM is followed by more NREM before the next REM (short-term REM homeostasis)
nodes.text: The best-replicated sequence finding in rodents (Vivaldi 1994, Benington & Heller 1994, Park 2021).

nodes.title: REM propensity builds with NREM since the last REM, and each REM empties it whatever its length
nodes.text: REM propensity rises with NREM accumulated since the last REM, peaking after ~10–20 min (established), and one count of it, emptied by every REM bout, predicts NREM endings best (#32, #33). A REM-length-dependent discharge (the Park relation) is not better within the model family (#33, established), and no stable reach beyond the next cycle was found. Deeper recent NREM favours REM (candidate, LFP stage). Whether the wake since the last REM lowers a REM drive or marks arousal-prone periods is still not separated: the count's discount over a wake fits either reading. From r8 (step F1): the same count goes with a longer next REM bout (#48, established association, both scorings); brief awakenings are most frequent right after a REM and grow rarer as the count rises (#51; the 'failed REM attempts' prediction had the opposite sign); no shortening of inter-REM intervals within a sleep episode was detected (#53). Whether the count is a behavioural proxy for cortical NREM depth or a parallel process is the first LFP-stage test (n.lfp_l1).

nodes.title: Does the history survive interruptions — natural wakes and handled battery rounds?
nodes.text: Closest to the core hypothesis. Two ways to be robust to interruption: store where you are and resume, or keep the organisation in slow quantities that a wake barely changes. They differ in what happens after an interruption.

nodes.title: Carry-over: pre-wake history still predicts transitions after the wake
Reset: a wake erases the history; sleep after it starts fresh
nodes.text: Weakened for wakes < 2 min (#5). For wakes ≥ 7 min untested with power: #6 argues only against a fixed fresh state, with #6's selection caveat. In Step B's terms this is τ_w = 0: every wake, microarousals included, erases the count. The step at 7 min is h.carry.hard_reset.

changes.what: Read as τ_w = 0 (every wake erases): Step B, erasing at every wake is −1.6 % worse held out, 6/6 rats on both scorings (#5, #34); still weakened.

nodes.title: Store-and-resume: REM progress is kept through the wake and resumed afterwards
nodes.text: In Step B's terms the pause (τ_w = ∞): the count is frozen over a wake and continues after it.

nodes.text: Pre-wake NREM coefficient ≈ 0 in every wake bin where resumption predicts ≈ −0.3. nodes.text: Wakes under 2 min do not erase the history (established). nodes.title: A wake fades the count over ~5–10 min: brief wakes keep it, long wakes wipe it (not resumed); at night longer wakes delay REM further
nodes.text: Brief wakes keep the history (established); erasing the count at every wake is clearly worse (established). A wake ≥ 7 min is not resumed (established): a pause loses after long wakes. The count fades over a wake with a time constant of ~5–10 min (candidate strong), but a smooth discount and a step at ~7 min are not separable (the pre-registered comparison failed on FINAL; the 2–7-min middle is FINAL-only). Besides the NREM count, wall-clock time since the last REM adds (established, FINAL), its process unknown. At night longer wakes still push REM back (candidate), not separable from time of night; the delay is not mainly selection or post-wake fragility. Whether handling resets the count stays untested with power. From r8 (steps F1 / F2): within the dark, ln d holds beside hours since sunset on FINAL only (H5), the 2–7-min wakes are not two kinds for carry-over (H23, underpowered), and a new sleep site after a long wake does not detectably delay REM (H17, underpowered) — the night ramp stays wake length vs time of night, and step vs discount stays open. From r9 (part W): a memory of the last long wake, carried to the first REM and × dark, adds no held-out gain beyond the count, the preceding wake and the clock (#64); the ramp's direction is there, its predictive value beyond the model is not.

nodes.title: #43 REM missed before a morning round is repaid by a process the count rules do not contain; natural dawn wakes show no such repayment
nodes.text: D2: observed day-demeaned slope +0.34 (1 h) / +0.96 (3 h) on pass2med vs simulated without a REM deficit +0.005 / +0.01 (95 % range up to +0.28 / +0.54). D1: natural dawn wakes −0.02 [−0.21, +0.17] (41 windows, 4/6); with the same model the rounds +0.29 (p 0.0003). Low power at night (~1.5 min of expected REM in 3 h). Within the same simulation (Fable conflict review, 2026-10-09): the NREM make-up after morning rounds IS reproduced (+0.129 vs +0.167 observed) while the REM repayment is not (+0.005 vs +0.335) — the REM repayment is REM-specific and not a measurement artefact of the window method. Part G (r8; reading rule → stays Candidate, power): G1 D1's dawn null is not informative (MDS 0.49 analytic / 0.27 simulated vs the round slope 0.34) → dawn timing not excluded; G2 no handling-specific REM-entry shortfall against matched natural long wakes (≤ 3 animals); G3 the REM expected during the unrecorded gap does not absorb the pass2med slope (fall 3 % / 2 %), while on FINAL (no pre-round slope) the gap's expected REM itself predicts more REM after the round (+0.15 per min) — the scorings disagree on what is repaid; G4 a larger slope where the clock-only model predicts more REM entry at 1 h on pass2med only. Parts P / T (r9): with the arousal in the simulation FINAL's morning REM in 3 h stays above the range with the 3-h-blind base but is inside with the 6-h-blind base (base-dependent); pass2med's day-demeaned debt slope stays above with every variant and both bases (+0.34 / +0.96 vs ≤ +0.32 / ≤ +0.66) — the only robust REM residual, on fixed thresholds; residuals on different quantities → part Q (a REM-need variable) not run.
nodes.null_reading: The natural-dawn null (D1) is underpowered: the dawn debts are small (SD 1.3 vs 2.5 min for rounds), 3 h of night hold ~1.5 min of expected REM, and the 3-h horizon is inconclusive (9 windows): 'not seen' is not 'absent'. Part G1 confirms it: D1's minimal detectable slope (0.49 iid) exceeds the round slope (0.34).

nodes.text: Part S1 (r8): among first movers in NREM, the model's per-step waking propensity ranks who wakes within 60 s at AUC ≈ 0.6, and that comes from the clock and the time in the bout — the REM-entry count adds nothing (#45, established scoped negative, both scorings, 6/6; also with wakes < 15 s after the movement excluded). nodes.title: Within-event test: does each participant's own history predict who wakes, beyond its pre-event state and identity?
nodes.text: On the Phase-6 library (complete flags only). (1) Count the events in which some asleep participants wake and others do not: the within-event model draws its information from them. (2) Main model: event-stratified (conditional) logistic regression of woke60 on each participant's pre-event state and history at t0 — NREM since its last REM, wake share of the last 10 min, time since sleep onset, time in the current bout — and animal. Role (first / tight / loose / still) only in a secondary analysis: it is a response to the event and could block the path under test (astra review r1). (3) The same history terms at matched no-event co-sleep moments, to test history × event: event-specific vulnerability vs a general tendency to wake. Held out by day-half blocks; repeated on the fixed-threshold scores. Reuses the FINAL states and the library on this PC; no new extraction.

changes.what: Now step F H12 of the explore plan (P(wake within 60 s | movement) ~ count P + time since sleep onset + phase + group size, with the A5 controls): use the fitted count P (τ_w 10 min, κ 0) as the history term and pass2med as the check. Priority 1 → 2, behind the origin of #43.

Part S1 ran H12 at the population level: the count does not help rank which movements wake (#45); movers wake beyond the model (#46). nodes.title: #40 Simulating only the fitted rules, conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps, reproduces the rats' sleep — daily REM / NREM and their day-to-day variation, and the night → day pattern with day fixed effects
nodes.text: The count (emptied by REM, × exp(−d/10 min) over a wake), the smooth daily clock and a brief arousal before REM: 27 of 28 checks within the pre-registered tolerances (13/14 FINAL, 14/14 pass2med; '27/28 on each scoring' was a wording error, corrected in the report and the audit 2026-10-09). Daily REM 1.683 vs 1.694 h, SD 0.343 vs 0.342 (FINAL); REM share day / night 17.4 / 7.3 vs 17.4 / 6.8 %; latencies 5/6 cells (fail: night after 7–30-min wakes, FINAL, 14 episodes). Carry-over curve: same sign in every bin with a clear observed effect. Night → day slope with day fixed effects (within day, between animals; the pre-registered term): NREM simulated −0.13 / −0.09 vs observed −0.12 / −0.10; REM inside the simulated range on both scorings. v1 → v2 correction: short wakes are sampled with their next state (12–15 % of REM bouts follow a ≤ 10-s wake).
nodes.scope: generative check, 100 replicates, both scorings; conditional on the observed waking; the night → day pattern only with day fixed effects
nodes.allowed: A model with no daily budget — only the count, the daily clock and the observed times the rats were awake — reproduced how much REM and NREM they had each day and how much that varied from day to day.
nodes.forbidden: 'There is no REM budget' (a budget model was not fitted; the rules suffice given the observed waking); claims independent of the observed waking pattern (the simulation is conditional on it). 'The model reproduces the night → next-day REM covariance across days'; 'there is no within-animal REM balance' (the day-FE REM test is weak; with a linear day term the FINAL REM slope −1.16 lies outside the simulated range, a between-day, FINAL-only residual kept as an open ledger item) (Fable conflict review, 2026-10-09).

nodes.title: A few rules generate the sleep without a budget: the count beats momentum, an NREM homeostat adds nothing, only the post-round REM repayment is missing
nodes.text: One count since the last REM (emptied by REM, fading over a wake), a smooth daily clock and a brief arousal before REM, simulated conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps, reproduce daily REM and NREM and their day-to-day variation, the day/night REM share and entry rate, first-REM latencies (5/6 cells), the carry-over curve and the night → day pattern with day fixed effects (#40, established; the simulator was corrected v1 → v2 after the first run; with a linear day term a between-day REM residual remains on FINAL, an open ledger item). The count beats a momentum model held out (#41); an hour-scale NREM homeostat adds nothing to NREM endings (#42). The rules do not produce the REM repayment after morning rounds (#43, candidate). Not tested: a daily REM quota (H9), REM maintenance terms (H7, H8); latencies after the longest night wakes run short without a wall-clock term (post hoc). A ripple rival (r7, next stage LFP): at the scale of the REM cycle, NREM ripples add no REM-entry information beyond the count, the clock and the wake history (#54, bounded at ~0.05 %; sleep onset untested); the ripple counter's small gain is the ripple poverty of short REM-ending NREM bouts (#55, a description) — see q.ripples. From r8 (step F1): REM already taken that day adds nothing to REM entry beyond the count (#52, no within-day quota in the transitions); the same count predicts the next REM bout's duration (#48), which the simulator's history-free REM durations and exits do not contain (not revised: the behaviour stage is closed). From r9: Step E's checks stay 13/14 (FINAL) and 14/14 (pass2med) with the post-round arousal (P3, T3 on pass2med) and with the long-wake term (W2 (iii)); a long-wake memory adds no held-out gain (#64). The rules, never shown a round, predict the post-round amounts but not its acute response (q.perturbation).

nodes.title: Do NREM sharp-wave ripples carry REM-entry information beyond the count — is the ripple-rich / REM-poor reciprocity a link or shared drivers?
nodes.text: The user (2026-10-09): add the NREM ripple rate to the REM-entry model as a candidate predictor, never as a nap or REM criterion ('the same NREM duration may contain different hippocampal activity'), and test held-out gain with information from before each step only. The question behind it: is 'ripple-rich, REM-poor' (naps, the early main sleep) a coincidence of the clock and sleep pressure, or a link? Reference model = Step B's B-full with the count fixed at P_tw600_k0 (count + clock + experiment day + L1 wake history + animal), both scorings. Pre-registered with the model's owner (Amendment 1); artifact checks (Amendment 2) and the follow-up after a read-only Fable audit (Amendment 3) were each written before they ran. Ripples are an LFP feature: their claims belong to the next stage (LFP) by the 2026-10-08 scope rule.

nodes.title: Link: NREM ripples carry REM-entry information beyond the count — REM readiness tracks what happened in NREM, not only how much of it
nodes.text: The user's idea, tested as pre-registered: only a held-out gain from the ripple rate with its window ending 60 s before the step (the readiness test) supports it; a gain at lag 0 can be the transition already under way. The ripple counter (ripples instead of NREM minutes, P's bookkeeping) was to be read as 'how much NREM vs what happened in it' only if the readiness test held.

nodes.title: Shared drivers: once the count, the daily clock and the wake history are known, NREM ripples add nothing about REM entry — so the reciprocity need not be a link
nodes.text: The plan's alternative ('a coincidence of the clock and sleep pressure'): the ripple rate and REM share both follow the time of day, NREM depth and the count, so the macro reciprocity needs no ripple → REM-entry link. Predictive level only; says nothing about what ripples do otherwise.

nodes.title: Scorer's cut: the ripple poverty of short REM-ending NREM bouts reflects how the scorer cuts REM episodes into REM and brief NREM labels
nodes.text: Named by the Fable audit (plan Amendment 3) and kept in #55: the scorer's NREM / REM call and the ripple detector read the same LFP, so brief 'NREM' labels inside a REM episode can be ripple-poor because their LFP is REM-like, not because the rat was in a different kind of NREM.

nodes.title: Physiology: brief NREM stretches between REM bouts of one episode are genuinely ripple-poor — a property of REM episodes, not of the scorer
nodes.text: The alternative to the scorer's cut, named by this map (r7) from #55's 'not separable' clause: the short NREM returns inside a REM episode would be real NREM of a different kind (e.g. light or intermediate sleep), poor in ripples. It would make the ripple counter's gain a real within-episode signal, not a scoring artefact.

nodes.title: Depth: what the ripple counter carries about REM entry is NREM depth, not ripples as such
nodes.text: Pre-registered as artifact check (iii) (K4: the discount-weighted mean NREM depth since the last REM, the scorer's raw spectral slope) and re-run with a same-subset baseline after the Fable audit (K4b). 'Carried by depth' needs the ripple term to fail beyond depth while it holds alone on the same subset.

nodes.title: Reverse link: the REM drive that the count tracks also lowers the NREM ripple rate — a link that a held-out test beyond the count cannot see
nodes.text: Proposed by this map (r7), not by a report. #54 is a predictive null beyond the count: if the process the count tracks also suppressed ripples, ripples would carry nothing beyond the count either, so #54 cannot separate this from ripples and REM merely sharing the clock and depth. Across the main sleep the ripple rate falls (1.11 → 0.87 × the block mean) while REM per NREM rises (0.08 → 0.21), together with depth and the clock (M1). Discriminator: the ripple rate against the count at matched clock, depth and time in the bout (n.rip_rate_vs_count).

nodes.title: Within long NREM bouts a last-minute ripple dip precedes REM and carries transition-local held-out information beyond the count — not readiness
nodes.text: From the Fable review r7: naps R3 describes a pooled last-minute dip before REM in runs ≥ 5 min, but no held-out test of a last-minute term within long bouts exists (T1 is a 10-min window, K7's ρ is cumulative since the last REM, K8 compares whole-bout rates). Even if it held it would be the transition under way, not REM readiness; a dip can also be the loss of detections in intermediate sleep. Untested.

nodes.title: Naps report R3: in NREM runs ≥ 5 min, the last-minute ripple rate relative to the run's own earlier rate is lower before REM than before WAKE (6/6)
nodes.text: Method: NREM runs ≥ 300 s followed directly by ≥ 30 s of REM or WAKE, anchored at the run's end, each with ≥ 200 ripple-eligible NREM s; events and eligible seconds pooled per animal × outcome; ratio = rate in the last 60 s / rate at −300…−120 s of the same runs; '6/6' = animals whose REM ratio − WAKE ratio < 0. Transitions REM / WAKE: SF07 106 / 53, SF08 101 / 52, SF09 100 / 63, SF10 184 / 49, SF11 9 / 8, SF12 102 / 46 (SF11 rests on 17). Kept events: REM − WAKE −0.14 (animal-level p 0.025), 6/6; all detected NREM events −0.09 (p 0.042), 6/6. The report's limits: the last seconds of NREM before REM are intermediate sleep, the 1-s scoring can blur the boundary, and the detector excludes REM seconds. Pooled, not per bout; no held-out test. Not a claim-audit entry: the allowed / forbidden wording below is the Fable review r7's. A different quantity from #55's K8 (whole-bout rates): c.pre_rem_drop resolved.

nodes.title: #54 At the scale of the REM cycle, NREM ripples add no REM-entry information beyond the count, the clock and the wake history
nodes.text: T1: the 10-min ripple rate at lags 0 / 60 / 120 s gives no held-out gain on either scoring (primary, lag 60 s, all events: −0.006 % [−0.036, +0.021] FINAL, +0.019 % [−0.041, +0.106] pass2med; bound ~0.05 %); in sample its REM coefficient is slightly positive (+0.10 per SD at 60 s), not negative. Ripples older than the last minute add nothing: the lagged ρ = ln((C + 0.5)/(P + 0.5)) ≈ 0 (−0.010 % / +0.001 %), also on steps ≥ 60 s into a bout where the lag can see (K7: −0.007 % / +0.031 %). Scope: 5 test animals (SF11 only in training); sleep-onset NREM after long wakes not tested (≥ 3 min NREM in the past 12 min required).

nodes.null_reading: A bounded null within scope, not 'no effect': the T1 CIs exclude a held-out gain above ~0.05 % from a linear 10-min window rate at lags 0–120 s, and the lagged counter adds nothing where the lag can see. Untested: sleep-onset NREM after long wakes, other or non-linear ripple features, SF11 (training only). The depth control is inconclusive, so 'not beyond depth' is not claimed.
nodes.allowed: At the scale of the REM cycle, NREM ripples added no REM-entry information beyond the NREM count, the clock and the wake history: no held-out gain above ~0.05 % from the recent ripple rate, and none from ripples older than the last minute.

nodes.text: Ripple counter C (P's bookkeeping, events instead of minutes): C replacing P −0.33 % / −0.30 %, B + ρ −0.33 % / −0.28 %, 4–5/5. nodes.title: At the REM-cycle scale ripples add nothing beyond the count (bounded); the ripple counter's small gain comes from ripple-poor short REM-ending NREM bouts — scorer's cut or physiology, not separated
nodes.text: Established (bounded negative, both scorings): at the scale of the REM cycle, NREM ripples add no REM-entry information beyond the count, the clock and the wake history — no held-out gain above ~0.05 % from the recent ripple rate, none from ripples older than the last minute (#54). Established as a description: short NREM bouts that end in REM (40 % of REM entries, often between REM bouts of one episode) are ripple-poor, and that poverty carries the ripple counter's small held-out gain, confined to the first one to two minutes of NREM bouts; in long bouts the whole-bout ripple rate before REM equals that before waking (#55). It is not separable from how the scorer cuts REM episodes (scorer and detector read the same LFP). The Amendment-2 reading — a transition-local ripple drop as REM begins — is withdrawn (r.rip_a2, superseded). Whether a last-minute ripple dip exists within long bouts and carries held-out information was not tested (T1 is a 10-min window, K7's ρ is cumulative since the last REM); naps R3 is a pooled within-run description of such a dip (ledger; a different quantity from K8, c.pre_rem_drop resolved). The depth control is inconclusive and counts for neither side. The macro reciprocity (ripple-rich naps and early main sleep are REM-poor; ρ −0.54, 6/6) is a ledger description; that drivers the model already has account for it is the report's reading, consistent with #54, not an audited claim. Limits: one cohort, 5 test animals (SF11 only in training), sleep-onset NREM after long wakes untested, ripple counts are not replay content. All ripple claims belong to the next stage (LFP).

nodes.text: Sample the NREM bouts ≤ 60 s that end in REM (40 % of REM entries) and matched short bouts that end in WAKE, per animal and on both scorings; read each blind to its outcome with measures the scorer's NREM / REM call does not use or uses differently: the user's manual reading of the LFP (as in n.manual_kappa), spindle / delta-wave / theta content on fixed channels, the head IMU; and count ripples with detection that does not depend on the state call. outcomes.if: Most short REM-ending 'NREM' bouts read as REM or intermediate sleep on the independent measures
outcomes.then: #55's signal is the scorer's cut inside REM episodes: the ripple counter's gain is a scoring artefact and the ripple branch reduces to #54's bounded null; the first-minute REM peak that #3 forbids reading as a permissive state reads as REM fragmentation.

outcomes.then: Ripple-poor brief NREM between REM bouts is a physiological feature of REM episodes (candidate, LFP stage); the ripple counter carries a real within-episode signal.

outcomes.if: The independent reads disagree with each other
outcomes.then: Scorer's cut vs physiology stays open; manual κ on these bouts comes first.

nodes.title: Does a last-minute ripple dip exist within long bouts, and does it carry held-out information?
nodes.text: Proposed by the Fable review r7, after c.pre_rem_drop (R3 and K8 measure different quantities; no held-out test of a last-minute term within long bouts exists). (a) Existence: the per-bout R3 ratio (last 60 s / the bout's own −300…−120 s rate) in K8's bout set (2–5 min and > 5 min), both scorings, ALL and KEPT events, per-bout values with an animal-level test, matched on depth z and clock. (c) Control: repeat (a) on the seconds before the first theta-flagged or IMU-movement second, to separate a dip from the loss of detections in intermediate sleep. LFP stage.

outcomes.if: (a) No dip within long bouts
outcomes.then: R3's pooled dip was diluted noise; #54 and #55 stay as they are.

outcomes.if: (b) holds on both scorings (CI < 0, ≥ 4/5 animals)
outcomes.then: A new candidate: transition-local information within long bouts beyond the count — still not readiness; (c) says whether it is a dip or lost detections in intermediate sleep.

nodes.title: #56 The extra waking after a battery round is well described by an arousal that raises the NREM → WAKE odds about 1.7-fold at the start of the post-round record and decays over 20–40 min
nodes.text: a = 0.43–0.64, τ_A = 20 or 40 min in both halves, both bases, both scorings. Cross-fitted first-hour WAKE O/E 1.26 → 1.04 [0.89, 1.25] (FINAL) and 1.34 → 1.05 [0.96, 1.17] (pass2med). Held-out log-loss on post-round steps −0.23 % [−0.44, −0.06], 5/6 (pass2med); −0.11 % [−0.39, +0.12], 6/6 (FINAL, CI crosses 0). Step E's checks unchanged with it (13/14, 14/14). Part T: with a 6-h-blind base the first-hour WAKE O/E is again restored (1.21 → 1.03, 1.29 → 1.05); over 0–6 h the gain is diluted and n.s. The window starts at the release into the paddock (#59); the waking excess sits before the first REM (WAKE O/E ~1.5, #61).

nodes.allowed: After a battery round the rats' chance of waking from NREM was raised about 1.7-fold at first and returned to normal within about half an hour to an hour; a term fitted on other rounds predicted this.

nodes.title: #57 The arousal does not explain the later first REM after rounds: with the measured waking excess in the simulation, the first REM still comes later than simulated
nodes.text: P2, 100 cross-fitted replicates: first-REM KM median FINAL morning 30.8 min vs 11.3–31.9 (inside at the edge), evening 211 vs 34–203 min; pass2med morning 30.7 vs 8.5–25.3, evening 206 vs 26–166 min; the arousal moved the simulated ranges by 1–3 min. Part T: with a 6-h-blind base and a one- or two-phase arousal, still 3 of 4 cells outside; the sleep recovered after the first hour that the model misses is mostly NREM. Part L: the delay sits mostly in the records that open with ~2 min scored NREM after release (#59); conditional on the observed states up to sleep onset the latency after onset is reproduced on FINAL and, in records that start awake (post hoc), on both scorings except pass2med evening without the arousal; the remaining REM-side piece is pass2med's evening NREM clock (#60). Part H: from the first NREM after the house entry the morning first-REM latency is reproduced on both scorings; the morning delay was the field period after release. The clause 'the delay is REM-side' (parts S / P) is withdrawn (the user, 2026-10-10, following part L); the S and P reports' reading sections are annotated accordingly since 2026-10-10 (c.rem_side).
nodes.scope: pre-registered test allowed to fail, failed on both scorings

'The delay is REM-side' (part L: mostly the records that open with scored NREM; only pass2med's evening NREM clock remains, #60).

nodes.title: #58 A delayed calm phase of waking of the tested form adds nothing held out beyond the single decaying arousal, and does not produce the sleep recovered in the following hours
nodes.text: T1: two-phase vs one-phase on post-round steps 0–6 h +0.005 % [−0.076, +0.088], 3/6 (FINAL) / +0.009 % [−0.029, +0.048], 2/6 (pass2med); b = −0.27 (se 0.05) in-sample on FINAL (both halves < 0; held out it over-corrects hours 3–6, WAKE O/E 1.08), ≈ 0 on pass2med. T2: REM / NREM minutes inside of 12, two-phase 9 / 11 = one-phase 9 / 11. The tested form: b (s/τ₂) e^(1 − s/τ₂) on the release clock. Part H: with the house-entry clock, waking 1–3 h after entry is below the model on both scorings (#63) — a calm phase is visible descriptively; the tested term still had no held-out gain.
nodes.scope: scoped negative, held out, both scorings; the tested two-phase form on the release clock only
nodes.null_reading: A precise null for the tested form within scope (two- vs one-phase within ±0.09 % on both scorings); FINAL's in-sample b = −0.27 and the entry-clock calm phase (#63) leave a calm phase of another form or clock open.

nodes.title: #59 A post-round recording starts when the rat is released into the paddock; about half open with ~2 min scored NREM, after which the rat wakes and later enters its house on its own; the first-REM delay (#57) sits mostly in these records
nodes.text: The field operator (the user, 2026-10-10): the formal recording starts when the rat is released into the paddock; short indoor tests (< 1 min) are separate sessions; the earlier reading 'Record Start before placement' (recording-inquiry, 2026-10-09) meant before release from the experimenter into the field, not before the house, and is withdrawn. On 09-05 the rats entered their houses 2.7–16.7 min after their Start (WISER vs the field-PC Starts). 49 / 94 (FINAL), 51 / 94 (pass2med) post-round records begin with an NREM bout (median 133 s, IQR 65–328), vs 20 % / 31 % of the other records; a median 5 min of WAKE in the first 10 min. In the post-hoc subset that starts awake the latency after sleep onset is reproduced (conditional simulation) in the morning on both scorings and in the evening on FINAL, and the full set's late first awakening after onset disappears. Part H: the opening NREM is scored while the rat is motionless in the field (#62); house entry median 5.3 min after release.

nodes.text: Check 2: REM-entry O/E before vs after the record's first REM: FINAL 1.16 [0.98, 1.49] vs 1.04 [0.90, 1.24]; pass2med 0.81 [0.69, 0.99] vs 0.88 [0.78, 0.99] (both ~15 % low, as after natural long wakes, 0.85 / 0.87). nodes.title: #62 The ~2 min of NREM that opens about half the post-round records is scored while the rat lies motionless in the field after release, before it enters a house
nodes.text: H4, opening NREM bouts (median 133 s; 49 / 51): head IMU still in 99–100 % of usable seconds vs 97–98 % in length-matched NREM in a house and 1–2 % in field WAKE; VeDBA ratio to matched NREM 1.00 / 0.85; WISER: 0 % in a house, maximum displacement 7.4–7.7 in (jitter level; house NREM 4.7–5.3 in, field WAKE 372 in). Scorer-validity risk (Fable plateau audit, 2026-10-10): the pre-registered rule separated 'settling' from a scorer-edge artefact by head stillness only; awake immobility passes the same rule, so if the opening bouts are awake immobility scored as NREM, every first-hour post-round number (#44, #56, #63) carries it — an LFP check of the opening bouts (delta / slope and spindle power vs the same animal's house NREM) is required, with the user's video review.

nodes.text: H1: field before entry WAKE O/E 1.73 [1.35, 2.21] (FINAL) / 1.65 [1.33, 2.11] (pass2med); first hour after entry 1.26 [1.01, 1.58] / 1.34 [1.18, 1.52]; 1–3 h after entry 0.84 [0.71, 0.99] / 0.87 [0.76, 0.98] (with the release clock, S2, the CIs had touched 1). nodes.title: #64 A memory of the last long wake (≥ 7 min, carried to the first REM, and its interaction with darkness) does not improve the prediction of NREM endings beyond the count, the preceding wake and the clock
nodes.text: W1: B-full + {ln(1 + LW), × dark} vs B-full −0.016 % [−0.162, +0.093], 3/6 (FINAL); −0.031 % [−0.113, +0.035], 5/6 (pass2med); ln(1 + LW) alone +0.061 % / +0.012 %. W2: with the term FINAL's evening latency after the house entry comes inside, not pass2med's (#60); Step E's checks stay 13/14 and 14/14.

nodes.title: H2: whether the post-round arousal follows the release clock or the house-entry clock is unresolved
nodes.text: Post-entry steps, part P's one-phase arousal with the release vs the entry clock: Δ held-out log-loss (entry − release) −0.018 % [−0.114, +0.082], entry better 4/6 (FINAL); +0.006 % [−0.034, +0.050], 2/6 (pass2med). The two clocks differ by minutes against τ_A of 20–40 min, so low power was expected (plan §13). Not an audited claim.
nodes.null_reading: Underpowered by design: the clocks differ by a median 5 min against an arousal decaying over 20–40 min; not evidence that the clock does not matter.

nodes.title: The rules predict the post-round amounts, not the acute response: waking highest in the field, still raised in the house, then a calm phase; the morning REM delay is the field period; an evening NREM-clock delay on fixed thresholds (candidate)
nodes.text: Established: rules never shown a round predict the REM and NREM amounts over 3–6 h after it (#47), but not its stability or timing. A post-round recording starts at the rat's release into the paddock (#59). Waking from NREM is highest in the minutes in the field before the rat enters its house, still raised for the first hour in the house, and below the prediction 1–3 h after entry (#63); after natural long wakes it is as predicted (#44); the excess sits before the first REM, and the first REM entry itself is not specially mispredicted (#61). Adding the measured waking to the simulation does not reproduce the later first REM (#57): the delay sits mostly in the records that open with ~2 min scored NREM while the rat lies motionless in the field (#59, #62), and from the first NREM in the house the morning first REM is reproduced — the morning delay is the field period. 'The delay is REM-side' is withdrawn. A calm phase of the tested two-phase form adds nothing held out (#58, scoped to that form), and a memory of the last long wake adds nothing (#64). Candidate: the waking excess is well described by a single arousal (odds ×1.7, decaying over 20–40 min, #56; held-out gain on pass2med only); after evening rounds the first REM needs more NREM than predicted (#60: pass2med strong, FINAL at the edge). Not separated: what causes the arousal (handling vs the release context; the release vs entry clock, H2), whether the opening NREM is sleep or awake immobility (#62's scorer-validity risk — if immobility, #44 / #56 / #63's first-hour numbers carry it), and whether the evening delay is pre-transition depth or a theta scoring lag (LFP stage).

nodes.title: LFP stage L1 (the decisive step): P only vs depth only vs P + depth vs P + depth + depth × dark, on identical held-out steps, REM and WAKE outcomes separately; depth as an outcome
nodes.text: Pre-registered in the LFP-stage plan (2026-10-10, written before any result; the user's GO after the Fable plateau audit). Multinomial B-full base; past depth from n.depth_lfp (non-scorer site, lag [t−150, t−30) s, 1-h-shifted negative control); forward-chained folds, both scorings, animal rule ≥ n − 1 of n; SF11 to 09-07 06:10, SF12 to 09-10 14:53:45, probe moves as hard block boundaries; naps and post-round onsets reported separately where clock and time since sleep onset decouple. Runs after the user confirms the sites.

outcomes.if: (b) P + depth vs depth n.s. on both scorings AND depth only ≤ P only
outcomes.then: The count is a behavioural proxy for cortical NREM depth: the count rules become a depth rule; #32's 'one counter' reads as depth (h.drive.p_proxy supported).

outcomes.if: (c) depth adds to P (CI < 0, ≥ n − 1 animals, control ≈ 0) AND P + depth beats depth
outcomes.then: Two processes: the count and NREM depth each carry REM-entry information (h.drive.two_processes); #4 moves toward established.

outcomes.if: (a) fails: depth adds nothing beyond P on both scorings
outcomes.then: #4 was scorer circularity or is contained in the count; depth is weakened as a separate driver.

outcomes.if: (d) the dark coefficient falls AND depth × dark gives held-out gain
outcomes.then: The night gain runs partly through NREM depth (h.dn.night_via_depth); a smaller dark coefficient alone is reported as reallocation only.

outcomes.if: (e) future depth rises with P at the same clock and prior wake, held out, sign ≥ n − 1
outcomes.then: Depth reads the same homeostat as the count (h.drive.depth_tracks_count).

nodes.title: LFP stage L2(c): is the opening field NREM sleep or awake immobility? — ON HOLD until the user's manual video labels
nodes.text: Required by the plan (#62's scorer-validity risk) and first in its order, but on hold (the user, 2026-10-10) until the user's manual video labels of the opening episodes exist; the episode list is part H's H4 table. 'NREM-like' = depth within 0.5 SD of the matched house NREM AND theta / delta below the quiet-wake median.

outcomes.if: ≥ 70 % of the opening bouts are NREM-like (and the video labels agree)
outcomes.then: The opening bouts are sleep: the rats fall asleep in the field right after release (h.pert.open_sleep supported); #44 / #56 / #63's first-hour numbers stand.

outcomes.then: Awake immobility scored as NREM: a scorer-validity ledger item for #44, #56 and #63, whose first-hour numbers are recomputed without the opening bouts as a sensitivity (h.pert.open_immobility supported).

nodes.title: A generative model that produces the long wakes itself (unconditional 24-h simulation): do the daily REM / NREM regularity and the 12-day drift emerge?
nodes.text: Recommended by the Fable plateau audit as a parallel, time-boxed project with pre-registered checks, not a gate for the LFP stage; the LFP-stage plan runs it outside the stage under its own plan (not written yet). Tests the organising idea that daily totals are regular because the inputs are regular (#40 is conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps, so the conditioning does the work). It can fail for reasons unrelated to the scheduler (long wakes are driven by foraging, housemates, weather, handling).

outcomes.if: With the long wakes generated, the daily REM / NREM means and SDs (and the #30 drift) emerge within the pre-registered tolerances
outcomes.then: 'Regular inputs, no budget' gains (h.core.regular_inputs supported, candidate); #40's sufficiency no longer rests on the observed waking.

outcomes.if: They do not emerge
outcomes.then: #40's sufficiency rests on the conditioning on the observed waking; the regularity of the daily totals stays unexplained by the rules alone (informative fail).

nodes.title: SWR events for the ripple model: ALL detected NREM events primary, KEPT (flags applied) as sensitivity; the scorer and the detector read the same LFP
nodes.text: The lab's DetectSWR port with one boundary per animal × probe block. Covered seconds: session tier validated / good in the SWR quality guide, before use_until, outside the probe-advance settle windows; SF11's ripples only to 09-02 (~17:04). ALL = every detected event whose peak second is NREM in the scoring being modelled, flags ignored; KEPT drops theta- / REM-flagged events, which shares information with the scorer's REM call, so ALL decides. No event inside the predicted step enters.

nodes.title: Ripple-model subsets: steps whose preceding 12 min of NREM are ripple-covered (S1; S2 adds every NREM second since the last REM); 5 test animals, holds = CI < 0 and ≥ 4/5
nodes.text: S1 needs ≥ 3 min of NREM in each window and a causal block normaliser (≥ 30 min of covered block NREM), so steps after an uncovered stretch, early in a block, or at sleep onset after a long wake are lost (FINAL: 127 461 of 179 668 steps). SF11's ripples end inside the six train-only blocks, so it has no test steps.

sources.anchor: S1 keeps the steps whose preceding 12 min are ripple-covered

nodes.title: Perturbation-blind models: B-full and the simulator fitted without the 3 h (part T: 6 h) after every usable round gap; per-step predictions held out by forward chaining; arousal terms fitted on waking only and cross-fitted over rounds by date parity
nodes.text: Round = a usable round gap (cause round_logged / round_inferred; ≤ 180 min with ≥ 1 h recorded on both sides); the first 6 day-half blocks are never predicted, so the per-step O/E use fewer events than the simulations. The simulations stay conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps (b.sim_conditional).

nodes.title: Post-round clocks start at the recording start = the rat's release into the paddock (field operator, 2026-10-10); the WISER house entry, a median 5.3 min later, is the second clock (part H)
nodes.text: Short indoor tests (< 1 min) are separate sessions. On 09-05 the rats entered their houses 2.7–16.7 min after their Start. House entry = the first WISER house visit within 60 min of release (default tracks, cohort-3 re-centred houses, 14-in buffer, hysteretic visits); 31 / 94 rounds have a visit already running at the start (released next to a house, or jitter within the buffer). Every post-round number before part H (S2, S3, parts P / T / L) is on the release clock, so its first hour includes the field period after release.

conflicts.title: Does a longer REM lengthen the following NREM interval?

sides.says: Single cycles: +0.07 [0.05, 0.10], 6/6; all cycles +0.01 (n.s.); pre-post-rule states −0.12.
Phase 1 cycles-ahead k = 1 (all REM cycles in a SLEEP, intervening terms controlled): −0.05 (n.s.), 3/6 — 'the classic k = 1 relation is not reproduced'.
Transition model: previous REM length adds a little (−0.31 %), sign depends on the other history terms; null in v1.

conflicts.resolution: Different quantities: where comparable (all cycles), v1 (+0.01) and Phase 1 k = 1 (−0.05) agree on ≈ 0; +0.07 is the single-cycle subset and −0.12 another scoring; v2 #4 is a hazard coefficient conditional on the window terms (+0.13 in M1, −0.04 in M2), not an interval claim. Sayable: v1 #8's allowed wording plus #18. Settling it needs the two-part rerun on three scorings (n.rem_length_two_part).
conflicts.resolved_by: Fable review r1 (v1 audit:43, Phase 1:75, v2 report:33 and 59)

conflicts.title: Does a long wake delay the next REM, given that REM minutes after a wake do not depend on its length?

sides.says: NREM before the first REM after a wake ≥ 7 min grows with ln(wake length): +0.26, 6/6 (cycles that reached REM).
REM minutes over 1–3 h after natural wakes do not depend on wake length on the same events (−0.08, n.s.).

conflicts.resolution: Compatible, not a conflict: different events (≥ 7 min vs mostly 2–7-min wakes), outcomes and selection. Arithmetic from the reported numbers (not a result): +0.26 per ln unit ≈ 3 min per doubling of a ~15-min first-REM latency ≈ 0.3 min less REM in the first hour, which the same-events null (−0.08 [−0.25, +0.09]) cannot detect. n.survival_long_wake measures both on the same events.
conflicts.resolved_by: Fable review r1 (Phase 2:24-27, Phase 3:130 and 151, Phase 3b:18)
conflicts.note: r2: #6 was split; the delay is now #6b (at night only) and the logic audit reads #6 and #12 as consistent (the hour after a long wake also carries extra NREM).

conflicts.title: Do the 10 min–3 h windows carry history beyond the since-last-REM quantities?

sides.says: v2: window terms (10 / 60 / 180 min) add −1.00 % on top of the clock baseline M0; ≈ −0.75 % beyond the anchors (no CI).
Phase 1: bands 10–720 min add +0.12 % [−0.05, +0.32] on top of the since-last-REM layer L2.

conflicts.resolution: Within precision the bands' information is a subset of L2's: they help on top of the current state alone (M3_720 vs M1 −0.40 %, holds) but not on top of L2. v2's 10-min window is Phase 1's current state (L1). The schedule audit supersedes v2 where they differ.
conflicts.resolved_by: data (Phase 1 lines 36 and 39; v2 report lines 20-21 and 37-38), premise corrected by the Fable review r1

conflicts.title: Do the history rules change with time of day?

sides.says: No: 2-harmonic history × phase adds +0.07 % (n.s.).
Yes, slightly: history × night −0.13 % [−0.28, −0.02], 13/15.

conflicts.resolution: The claim audit states that #15 supersedes v2's null (a night indicator vs a 2-harmonic interaction).

conflicts.title: Is the night → next-day REM trade-off robust?

sides.says: Pooled slope −0.98, p < 0.001.
Within-rat: REM −0.41 to −1.11, CIs mostly include 0; NREM robust.

conflicts.resolution: Phase 3b robustness (within-rat, both scorings) made REM the weaker part; the audit words #13 'clearly for NREM, weaker for REM'.
conflicts.note: r2: #13 itself was withdrawn as a balance (a cohort drift, #30); the REM version is revisited in c.night_day_rem.

conflicts.title: Does a housemate's movement wake the sleeping partner?

sides.says: Partner ~1.5× more likely to wake within 30 s (vs 60 s earlier).
Still partners: 20.3 % vs 19.5 % random co-sleep seconds; the extra waking lies in partners who also move.

conflicts.note: The claim audit treats #29d as refining #28c (#28c used a within-pair 60-s-earlier baseline and pooled followers with non-movers), and the Fable review agrees. The astra review objects: 'still' is defined after the event, so a partner woken by the mover, which tends to move, is counted as a follower; the two baselines and populations are not equivalent. Not settled: a test with roles defined before the event (or by distance) is needed.

conflicts.title: Does a REM shortfall persist within continuous sleep?

sides.says: FINAL: −0.11 / −0.28 per min of debt (1 h / 3 h), 5/6 negative.
Fixed thresholds: +0.003 / +0.001.

conflicts.resolution: A per-session threshold error lasts a whole session and produces exactly this persistence; withdrawn as a scoring artefact (plan Amendment 2).

conflicts.title: Where is the REM refractory low point?

sides.says: Phase 1 figure: a 30-s low point.
Phase 2 C2: lowest hazard at 2–3 min of NREM since the last REM.

conflicts.resolution: The Phase 1 figure compared bouts starting at different accumulated NREM; mislabelled and replaced by C2 (Amendment 1).

conflicts.title: Does the 'running totals' result show that the detailed sequence is not needed?

sides.says: Audit #2 allowed wording: 'the sleep system does not need the detailed sequence'.
The Phase-1 bands are shares of REM / wake per window; the order of states was not tested (astra review r1).

conflicts.note: The audit wording may be broader than the test. The map keeps the audit status and flags the wording for the user. r6: #41 tested the order of the last two bouts only (momentum loses to the count, with a small FINAL-only residual); longer orders are still untested, and the #2 wording is unchanged in the audit.

conflicts.title: Does the long-wake delay last only about one cycle?

sides.says: Audit #6 allowed wording: 'The effect lasted about one cycle' (2nd REM +0.22 n.s., 3rd 0).
2nd REM +0.22, SE 0.15 (CI ≈ −0.06 to +0.51), n 231: underpowered, compatible with a longer effect (astra review r1).

conflicts.note: The 'not resumed' part rests on a precise null (pre-wake NREM −0.02, SE 0.016) and stands within scope; the 'one cycle' part is a non-detection.

conflicts.title: Is there a pre-REM ripple dip within long NREM bouts — does naps report R3 still stand as a description now that the ripple model withdrew 'a transition-local drop'?
conflicts.resolution: Different quantities. R3 = the last-60-s ripple rate ÷ the same runs' −300…−120 s rate, NREM runs ≥ 300 s anchored at the run's end, pooled per animal × outcome (ephys/swr_rem_naps.py). K8 = the whole-bout rate before the last step: a −14 % last minute diluted over ≥ 5 min is ≤ −3 %, and K8's > 5-min medians differ by −2.1 / −2.4 % (same sign and size). K7's ρ is cumulative since the last REM and T1 is a 10-min window, so no held-out test of a last-minute term within long bouts exists. #55 forbids only the predictive / transition-local READING, not the measurement: R3 stands as a ledger description with its own allowed / forbidden wording (r.swr_r3); #55's long-bout statement is the whole-bout rate (r.s55, j.ripples.r7). The open question went to n.rip_last_minute.

sides.says: Naps report R3: in NREM runs ≥ 5 min, the last-60-s ripple rate relative to the run's own −300…−120 s rate is lower before REM than before WAKE: REM − WAKE −0.14 (p 0.025), 6/6; all events −0.09 (p 0.042), 6/6. The ripple-model report still states it as a premise: 'Ripples also drop in the last minute before REM (6/6)' (its question, line 21) and 'a gain only at L = 0 is the transition already under way, since ripples drop in the last minute before REM' (its reading and limits, line 350).

Claim audit #55 forbids 'a pre-REM ripple drop as a predictive or transition-local signal' and 'ripples vanish as REM begins' (withdrawn after the Fable audit); the change log's revised reading says the signal 'is not a pre-REM ripple drop within longer bouts'; K8: in bouts longer than 5 min the whole-bout ripple rate before REM equals that before WAKE (74 vs 76 / 73 vs 75 per min); K7: no unlagged gain that holds on both scorings 60 s into a bout, none on either from 120 s.

conflicts.note: Possibly different quantities: R3 is a within-run last-minute ratio (a description, kept and all events), while #55 / K7 / K8 concern the counter's held-out gain and whole-bout rates. Not decided here: whether R3 stands as a description (with #55 forbidding only its predictive / transition-local reading) or is withdrawn too, and whether the ripple-model report's lines 21 and 350 should be revised. The map keeps R3 as a ledger description and uses no pre-REM drop in any judgment. (Sides quote the sources as they read when the conflict was opened.)

answers.aim: Lay out the whole sleep analysis so far as one logic: does sleep keep an internal history and reorganise NREM/REM after disturbance, and prepare the link to who keeps sleeping vs wakes in a shared event.
answers.answered: History shapes how NREM ends, is summarised by a few running quantities since the last REM, and survives brief wakes (all established). The night limits REM entry, not REM maintenance (established). REM coupling between housemates beyond shared timing was rejected, while fast movement coupling is strong and partly active.

Weakened: the no-history null; a within-cycle stage trade-off (the PI's first formulation); store-and-resume after long wakes; REM payback within continuous sleep; housemate REM coupling. answers.indistinguishable: Update vs a selection effect vs post-wake fragility for the long-wake delay (#6); NREM vs wall clock; a lower REM drive vs arousal-prone periods; payback vs timing shift; handling itself vs the round's long daytime wake; the night itself vs the long wake before naps; propagation vs a common trigger; contagion vs a shared drift to lighter sleep; day weather vs the day-order trend; and, for the new link, own history vs role/state vs animal trait, and event-specific vulnerability vs a general tendency to wake.
answers.next: Priority 1: the within-event history test on the Phase-6 library (n.within_event_history): first count the events where some participants wake and others do not; main model on pre-event state, history and animal (role only as a secondary analysis); then history × event against matched no-event moments. If history predicts waking more during events, the carried history also sets resilience to disturbance (core judgment extended); if equally without events, it sets a general tendency to wake; if only the animal predicts, who wakes is individual (not evidence that history plays no role); if only in NREM, NREM depth at the event (LFP) is next. answers.aim: Test whether NREM sharp-wave ripples carry REM-entry information beyond the count P (Step B's B-full at P_tw600_k0), the clock and the wake history, held out on both scorings — i.e. whether the macro 'ripple-rich naps / REM-poor nights' reciprocity is a link or shared drivers. Pre-registered with the model's owner; the artifact checks (Amendment 2) and the follow-up after a read-only Fable audit (Amendment 3) were each written before they ran.
answers.answered: At the scale of the REM cycle ripples add no REM-entry information beyond the count, the clock and the wake history (#54, Established, bounded at ~0.05 %): the recent 10-min ripple rate adds nothing at lags 0–120 s, and ripples older than the last minute add nothing, also where the lag can see (K7). The ripple counter's small held-out gain (−0.33 % / −0.30 %) is the ripple poverty of short NREM bouts that end in REM — 40 % of REM entries, often between REM bouts of one episode — confined to the first one to two minutes of NREM bouts (#55, Established as a description). The Amendment-2 reading (a transition-local drop: ripples vanish as REM begins) is withdrawn and kept only as superseded history (r.rip_a2). The depth control is inconclusive: the scorings disagree.
answers.supported_weakened: Weakened (established, bounded): a ripple → REM-readiness link at the REM-cycle scale. Supported (established, predictive, REM-cycle scale): shared drivers — once the count, the clock and the wake history are in, ripples add nothing about REM entry; that this accounts for the macro reciprocity is the report's reading, not an audited claim. Weakened: the precursor reading of the counter's gain (a pre-REM drop within longer bouts). The count model survives a ripple rival (j.model.r6 refined). Depth: neither way.
answers.indistinguishable: Whether the ripple-poor short REM-ending NREM bouts are the scorer's cuts inside REM episodes or genuinely ripple-poor brief NREM (scorer and detector read the same LFP); whether NREM depth carries the counter's gain (K4b: FINAL beyond depth holds, pass2med does not); whether the REM drive that the count tracks also lowers ripples (a link a predictive test beyond the count cannot see) vs ripples and REM sharing only the clock and depth; a ripple contribution that moves with the daily clock and is absorbed by it; sleep-onset NREM after long wakes (outside the subset); and whether a last-minute ripple dip exists within long bouts and carries held-out information — naps R3 is a pooled within-run description, a different quantity from K8's whole-bout rates (c.pre_rem_drop resolved by the Fable review r7), and no held-out test of a last-minute term exists.
answers.next: Top for this branch (LFP stage): n.rip_short_bouts — read the short REM-ending NREM bouts blind with independent state measures. If they read as REM or intermediate sleep, #55 is the scorer's cut: the ripple branch reduces to #54's bounded null (j.ripples.r7) and #3's first-minute REM peak reads as REM fragmentation (j.drive.r4). If they are genuine NREM and stay ripple-poor, ripple-poor brief NREM between REM bouts becomes a candidate physiological feature of REM episodes (j.ripples.r7). If the reads disagree, it stays open and manual κ comes first. n.depth_lfp (already priority 12 for #4) now also settles K4b: depth absorbing the gain on both scorings → h.rip.depth; surviving → beyond depth (j.ripples.r7). Then n.rip_last_minute (Fable review r7): no per-bout dip → R3 was diluted noise, #54 / #55 unchanged; a dip with a held-out null → a description without predictive value; a held-out gain on both scorings → a new candidate, transition-local information within long bouts, still not readiness (j.ripples.r7). n.rip_rate_vs_count separates a REM-drive → ripple link from shared drivers in the narrow sense (j.ripples.r7).

rounds.label: Sleep behaviour explore, Amendment 1: sleep stability and the battery rounds as a perturbation (S), the origin of #43 (G), the step-F batches (F1 sequence-only, F2 WISER / environment / social)

answers.aim: The user's question: can the count model predict sleep stability — which movements end in waking, and how sleep responds to the battery rounds, a systematic perturbation a true model should predict? Plus the origin of the post-round REM repayment (#43) and the step-F hypotheses on REM maintenance, the night ramp, a daily quota, the cycle structure, wake activity, housemates, warmth and rain — all with rules written before results.
answers.answered: The rules, never shown a round, predict the REM and NREM amounts over 3–6 h after it (#47) but not its stability: for about an hour NREM ends in waking ~1.3–1.45× as often as predicted, in all six rats, and not after natural long wakes (#44); the first REM comes later in wall time (#47). The count does not help rank which movements wake (#45); movers wake ~20 % more than predicted (#46, scorer circularity). #43 stays Candidate (power): dawn timing not excluded (G1), no handling-specific REM-entry shortfall (G2, ≤ 3 animals), the gap's REM loss does not absorb the pass2med slope while FINAL repays the gap's expected REM (G3), no consistent gate release (G4). F1: the same count predicts the next REM bout's duration (#48); MAs are most frequent right after a REM (#51); no daily REM quota in the transitions (#52); no within-episode shortening of inter-REM intervals (#53); night REM ends in waking more often (#49) and quick returns are rarer at night (#50), both Candidate. F2: nothing held on both scorings.
answers.supported_weakened: Supported: an acute post-round arousal the rules lack (established); the count goes with REM duration (established association); REM exits shift at night (candidate); role beyond the model (candidate). Weakened: the rules as a predictor of the round response (stability, timing); 'only REM entry is regulated' as stated (its maintenance half; conflict c.entry_only_wording, resolved 2026-10-10 by the audit owner's rewrite); the count as the history that gates who wakes (population level); pre-REM microarousals; ultradian progression; a daily REM quota; warmth via maintenance; a housemate's departure waking the partner.
answers.indistinguishable: What causes the post-round arousal (handling vs the release context); why the first REM comes later (part S read it as the extra waking — tested in r9); the origin of #43 (handling vs dawn timing vs the round's sleep loss vs a general REM deficit); the night ramp as wake length vs time of night (H5 FINAL only); step vs discount for 2–7-min wakes (H23 underpowered); wake activity vs the night for post-wake NREM (H4, path ≈ wake length); a new sleep site (H17) and rain (H22) — underpowered; quick returns rarer at night vs the shared REM-after-wake scorer rule (#50).
answers.next: Model the post-round response as dynamics before any REM-need rule (Amendment 2, part P): a decaying arousal fitted on waking only, cross-fitted and frozen, allowed to fail. If it restores the first-hour waking AND the simulated first REM, the delay is the arousal and no REM variable is needed (j.perturbation.r8 → r9); if the waking is restored but the delay stays, a REM-side (or other) process remains; a REM residual outside the simulated range in the same direction on both scorings would trigger part Q (j.compensation.r6). The within-event history test (n.within_event_history) stays open behind it.

rounds.label: Sleep behaviour explore, Amendments 2–6: perturbation dynamics after the battery rounds (P arousal, T two-phase, L where the delay is, H the house-entry clock) and the long-wake memory term (W); the behaviour stage closes

answers.aim: Model the post-round response as dynamics fitted on other data and frozen (P: a decaying arousal; T: a delayed calm phase), find where the later first REM sits (L: onset wait vs after onset vs the first entry; H: a clock at the rat's own house entry, and what the opening NREM is), and test one last behaviour-level term, a memory of the last long wake, against the evening delay and the night ramp (W).
answers.answered: A single arousal (odds ×1.7, decaying over 20–40 min, fitted on waking only) restores the first-hour waking held out (#56, candidate; log-loss gain on pass2med only) but not the later first REM (#57, established). A calm phase of the tested two-phase form adds nothing held out (#58, scoped to that form), though with the house-entry clock waking is below the model 1–3 h after entry on both scorings (#63). A post-round recording starts at the release into the paddock (#59, the field operator's correction); half open with ~2 min scored NREM while the rat lies motionless in the field (#62); waking is highest in the field before the house entry (#63); the delay sits mostly in those records, the first REM entry is not specially mispredicted (#61), and from the first NREM in the house the morning first REM is reproduced — the morning delay is the field period; 'REM-side' is withdrawn. After evening rounds the first REM needs more NREM than predicted (#60: pass2med strong, FINAL at the edge). A long-wake memory adds nothing (#64). FINAL's extra morning REM is base-dependent; pass2med's debt slope is the only robust REM residual (#43); part Q not run.
answers.supported_weakened: Supported: the arousal as one decaying term (candidate); a calm phase after the house entry (established, descriptive); the morning delay as the field period (established); an evening NREM-clock delay on fixed thresholds (candidate). Weakened: the waking as the explanation of the REM delay (established); a REM-side suppression (morning and the first entry, established; the evening stays open); the tested two-phase term (established, scoped); a general long-wake memory (established); the opening NREM as a scorer-edge artefact (established).
answers.indistinguishable: Whether the opening field NREM is sleep or awake immobility (#62's scorer-validity risk — if immobility, the first-hour numbers of #44 / #56 / #63 carry it); handling vs the release context as the arousal's cause (H2: the release vs entry clock unresolved); the evening delay as pre-transition depth vs a theta scoring lag vs a REM-side process; the night ramp as wake length vs time of night (#64 has its direction, no gain); the origin of #43.
answers.next: The Fable plateau audit: GO to the LFP stage (r10). The residuals left (#60, #62, #43) need LFP or video. First: the depth feature on a non-scorer site and L1, P vs depth vs P + depth; for this branch L2(c) (opening NREM: ≥ 70 % NREM-like → sleep; else a scorer-validity ledger item for #44 / #56 / #63) — on hold for the user's video labels — then L2(a) (#60 vs depth) and L2(b) (#60 vs a theta scoring lag), each changing j.perturbation.r9.
